fragments.text: Hello, wherever and whenever you're joining us. From morning in Mumbai to midnight in Montego Bay, Jamaica. Welcome to the sixth AI4IA conference. This year, we gather to commemorate the International Day for Universal Access to Information under our theme, AI Access in Focus. us. Access is not just about connectivity, it's about dignity, equity and empowerment. And so as artificial intelligence becomes more deeply embedded in our lives, let us begin with a truth that should never be a rebuttable presumption. Human dignity is and must always ways remain the first principle of AI governance. This foundational truth becomes even more critical as we confront this strange but serious reality that we are now creating machines

in our own image. And so in the years ahead, our reaction to AI will not be so much about the machine itself, it will be about our own moral conditioning. As AI agents become more integrated into our lives, we must ask what happens to our understanding of intimacy, empathy, and community when human-like technology becomes embedded in our already complicated social arrangements. What happens when artificial relationships feel easier, safer, and more available than human ones. Let me offer two imperatives for our collective reflection and action. First, as we deploy AI technology for efficiency and economic advancement, we must ensure this does not

come at the cost of human worth or the sustainability of our species. This is where the principle of human dignity must be most fiercely protected. It requires openness, inclusivity and enlightened access. People from all walks of life must have a say in the shaping of the future of AI. Second, we must teach moral literacy alongside digital media and information literacy. It's simply not good enough to show children and adults how to use artificial intelligence or to talk about the opportunities or the risks of artificial intelligence. No, that's not good enough. We must equally ensure that we help people to engage with artificial intelligence in ways that preserve their sense of self.

As you explore the more than 60 video presentations at your own pace in your own time zone, let us remember that AI access in focus is not just our theme. It is a call to action to ensure that access is shaped by ethics, guided by empathy, and directed towards human flourishing. In closing, I extend heartfelt thanks to the members of the UNESCO IFAP Working Group on Information Accessibility, which I have the honour of chairing, members of for IA planning committee and I salute in particular the dedicated AI for IA conference satellite organizers from India, Jamaica, Canada, Chile, Ukraine, Germany, the UK, South Africa and Zimbabwe. All of us supported by the UNESCO UNESCO IFAP Secretariat in Paris, the UNESCO Regional Office for Southern Africa, the UNESCO Cluster Office for the Caribbean, the Broadcasting Commission of Jamaica, and the University of Alberta. Thank you for being here.
